opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For 2026, I think the biggest shift will be AI moving from fluent output to output that is *verifiably correct*. We've spent the last few years marveling at how well models can talk, write, and code. The next frontier is whether we can trust what they produce, and mathematics is where that question gets sharpest.

So I'm especially excited about AI for mathematical reasoning combined with formal verification. When a model writes a proof in a language like Lean, you don't have to take its word for it. The proof checker either accepts it or it doesn't. That gives us a ground-truth signal, which is rare in AI. With that signal, you can build systems that generate conjectures, attempt proofs, check them, and learn from their failures in a closed loop. I expect 2026 to be the year this loop starts producing results that working mathematicians actually care about, not just competition problems but pieces of real research.

More broadly, I think we'll see the community take reasoning reliability much more seriously. Scaling pre-training gave us a lot, but much of the progress now comes from reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, better search at inference time, and agents that can work on a hard problem for hours rather than seconds. Math and code are the natural proving grounds because you can tell whether you succeeded.

And I hope 2026 is a year of collaboration rather than replacement. The most interesting outcome isn't AI solving math *instead of* mathematicians. It's mathematicians gaining a tireless collaborator that handles formalization, checks every step, and explores directions a human wouldn't have time for. If we get that right, verified reasoning won't stay in math. It will flow into software, chip design, and any domain where being correct really matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think 2026 is the year AI stops being judged on how impressive it sounds and starts being judged on whether it can actually be trusted to be right.

For most of the past few years, the headline capability has been fluency. Models write well, they explain well, they can mimic the texture of expert reasoning. But fluency is not correctness, and in a lot of domains that gap has been papered over by having a human in the loop to catch mistakes. What I expect in 2026 is that the frontier shifts toward verification. Can the system prove what it claims? Can it check its own work in a way that doesn't depend on a person reading every line?

That's why I'm so focused on math. Mathematics is the one place where "is this right?" has a definitive answer. If a model produces a proof and it's formally checked, there's no debate. So I think math becomes the proving ground for a much bigger question, which is whether AI can do genuinely rigorous reasoning rather than plausible reasoning. My bet is that in 2026 we'll see formal verification move from a niche research interest to something closer to infrastructure. More proofs written with AI assistance and machine-checked. More serious engagement from working mathematicians, not as a curiosity but as a tool they actually reach for.

The second thing I expect is that the conversation moves from models to systems. A single model answering a single prompt is not how hard problems get solved. Hard problems need search, they need decomposition, they need a loop of conjecture, attempt, failure, and revision. I think the interesting progress this year will come from how you orchestrate reasoning over hours or days, not just from a bigger base model.

And third, honestly, I expect some humility. I think we'll hit problems where the models are confidently wrong in ways that are subtle and expensive, and that will push the field toward building in guarantees rather than hoping for the best. I actually see that as healthy. The goal isn't an AI that sounds like a mathematician. The goal is an AI that can be wrong, discover that it's wrong, and fix it. If we make real progress on that in 2026, it matters far beyond math.

astra-6.text:
I think the big question for 2026 is how reliably AI can carry out longer, more complicated tasks. Getting one impressive answer is different from making progress over many steps, noticing when something has gone wrong, and correcting it.

I’m especially interested in what that could mean for mathematics and scientific research. Could AI help us explore an idea, identify a useful intermediate result, or find a mistake early? In those settings, being able to check the work matters as much as generating it.

So I’d expect progress, but probably uneven progress. The thing I’d watch is whether these systems become dependable collaborators in actual work, and how much human guidance they still need.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect 2026 to be about whether AI can turn impressive capabilities into reliable, useful work. It’s one thing for a model to solve a problem when you give it exactly the right context. It’s another for it to figure out what information it needs, work through several steps, and recognize when it’s made a mistake.

I’m particularly excited about AI for mathematics and scientific discovery. But I’d distinguish between getting a plausible answer and producing something we can actually verify. Progress on that second part could make these systems much more valuable.

The thing I’d watch is how much supervision they still need. Can you delegate a meaningful task and trust the result? I expect progress, but I’m less certain about how quickly we’ll get there.
